questions.stem: A nerve cell and a muscle cell from the same person look very different. How do their genes compare?
options: They contain the same genes, but different genes are expressed
They contain different genes, which is why they look different
The nerve cell contains more genes because it is more complex
The muscle cell has lost the genes that a nerve cell needs
questions.explanation: Cells in a multicellular organism come from one fertilised egg by mitosis, so they are genetically identical. They specialise because different genes are switched on (expressed) or off in each cell type.

questions.stem: Which process is responsible for cells in an embryo becoming specialised as skin, muscle or nerve cells?
options: Mutation, through changing the DNA sequence in each new type of cell
Meiosis, through halving the chromosomes in each cell
Fertilisation, through mixing genes from two parent cells
Differentiation, through switching particular genes on or off
questions.explanation: Differentiation produces specialised cells by controlling gene expression: each cell type makes a particular set of proteins. Mutation is a change in DNA, which is not how normal specialisation happens.

questions.stem: A repressor protein binds near a gene in liver cells but not in pancreas cells. What is the most likely result?
options: The gene is expressed more in liver cells than in pancreas cells
The gene mutates in liver cells and the protein changes shape
The gene is switched off in liver cells but can be expressed in pancreas cells
The gene is cut out of the DNA of liver cells but is kept in the pancreas cells
questions.explanation: Repressor proteins block transcription of a gene, switching it off, without changing or removing the DNA. Where the repressor is absent, the gene can be transcribed and its protein made.

questions.stem: Which list shows the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism, from simplest to most complex?
options: Cell, organ, tissue, system
Organ, tissue, cell, system
Cell, tissue, organ, system
Tissue, cell, system, organ
questions.explanation: Similar cells form tissues, different tissues form organs, and organs working together form systems. For example, cardiac muscle cells form cardiac muscle tissue, which is part of the heart in the circulatory system.

questions.stem: In a plant, which example correctly matches the level of organisation?
options: Root hair cell: a tissue of many cells
Shoot system: a single tissue made of only one type of cell
Leaf: an organ made of several different tissues
Xylem: a single cell that carries water
questions.explanation: A leaf is an organ because it contains several tissues, such as epidermis, mesophyll, xylem and phloem. Xylem is a tissue, a root hair cell is one cell, and the shoot system is a system of organs.

questions.stem: Which statement best shows that organ systems are interdependent?
options: Each organ belongs to exactly one system and never affects another
The digestive system makes its own oxygen for respiration
Muscles need oxygen from the respiratory system carried by the circulatory system
The skeletal system works alone to keep the body upright
questions.explanation: Organ systems rely on each other. For example, the respiratory system takes in oxygen, the circulatory system carries it to muscles, and the digestive system supplies glucose. The skeleton depends on muscles to move and on blood for supply.

questions.stem: Which set of features is typical of efficient exchange surfaces in animals?
options: Thick, dry, small surface area and a rich blood supply
Thin, dry, small surface area and few blood vessels
Thick, moist, large surface area and very few blood vessels
Thin, moist, large surface area and a rich blood supply
questions.explanation: A thin surface gives a short diffusion distance, moisture lets gases dissolve, a large area allows more exchange, and a rich blood supply keeps the concentration gradient steep.

questions.stem: Why does a rich blood supply increase the rate of oxygen uptake at the alveoli?
options: Blood releases its oxygen into the alveoli so that it can be breathed out
Blood carries oxygen away, keeping a steep concentration gradient
Blood pumps oxygen into the alveoli by active transport
Blood makes the alveolar walls thicker and stronger
questions.explanation: Flowing blood constantly removes oxygen that has diffused in, so the oxygen concentration in the blood stays lower than in the alveoli. This maintains a steep gradient for diffusion.

questions.stem: How do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the walls of the alveoli?
options: By endocytosis, in vesicles formed by the membrane
By diffusion, a passive process needing no extra energy
By active transport, using energy released by cellular respiration
By osmosis, along with water from the blood
questions.explanation: Respiratory gases diffuse down their concentration gradients: oxygen from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide from the blood into the alveoli. Diffusion is passive and needs no additional energy.

questions.stem: In emphysema, the walls between alveoli break down, forming fewer, larger air spaces. Why does a person with emphysema become breathless?
options: The blood supply to the alveoli is greatly increased
The air spaces fill with water and block all diffusion
The total surface area for gas exchange is reduced
The alveolar walls become too thin for any diffusion
questions.explanation: Fewer, larger air spaces have a smaller total surface area than many small alveoli, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood. Emphysema is strongly linked to smoking, an example of a lifestyle choice affecting an organ.

questions.stem: How are fish gills suited to gas exchange in water?
options: Many thin filaments give a large surface area with many capillaries
A thick waxy coating stops the water from ever touching the blood vessels
A few large air sacs store oxygen for later diffusion
Cartilage rods pump oxygen into the blood by active transport
questions.explanation: Gills have many thin filaments and plates that create a large, thin surface with a dense capillary network. Water flowing over them keeps a concentration gradient for oxygen to diffuse into the blood.

questions.stem: Through which structures do most gases enter and leave a leaf?
options: Root hairs
Stomata
Xylem vessels
Phloem sieve tubes
questions.explanation: Gases are exchanged mainly through stomata, small pores in the leaf surface opened and closed by guard cells. Gases then move through air spaces by diffusion, not through the plant's transport tissues.

questions.stem: How does carbon dioxide reach the palisade cells of a leaf on a sunny day?
options: It is made inside the palisade cells by photosynthesis
It diffuses in through stomata and through air spaces in the leaf
It is carried up from the roots in the xylem
It is pumped in by phloem from other leaves
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis lowers the carbon dioxide concentration inside the leaf, so carbon dioxide diffuses in through open stomata and through the spongy mesophyll air spaces. Gas movement does not use the transport system.

questions.stem: Why does a plant lose water when its stomata are open?
options: Water is pumped out of the guard cells by active transport
Water drains out of the phloem through the pores
Water is produced by respiration and released through the pores only at night
Water vapour diffuses out of the leaf through the open pores
questions.explanation: The air spaces in a leaf are saturated with water vapour, so when stomata open, water vapour diffuses out into the drier air. This loss of water is transpiration, the price of letting carbon dioxide in.

questions.stem: Nail varnish impressions show leaf A has 300 stomata per square millimetre on its lower surface and 20 on its upper surface. What is the most likely advantage?
options: The lower surface is shaded and cooler, so less water is lost through stomata
The upper surface needs no carbon dioxide, so fewer stomata are needed there
Stomata on the upper surface would let in too much light for photosynthesis
Most photosynthesis happens on the lower surface, which faces the sun
questions.explanation: Having most stomata on the shaded, cooler lower surface reduces water loss by evaporation while still allowing gas exchange. The upper part of the leaf still needs carbon dioxide, which diffuses through the air spaces.

questions.stem: Which organ is the main site of chemical digestion and absorption of nutrients in humans?
options: Oesophagus
Small intestine
Large intestine
Stomach
questions.explanation: Most chemical digestion is completed, and most nutrients are absorbed, in the small intestine, whose lining is folded into villi. The large intestine mainly absorbs water, and the oesophagus moves food to the stomach.

questions.stem: Which enzyme and product are correctly matched?
options: Protease: proteins to amino acids
Lipase: starch to glucose
Amylase: fats to fatty acids
Protease: starch to amino acid chains
questions.explanation: Proteases break proteins into amino acids, amylase breaks starch into sugars, and lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol. Each enzyme is specific to its substrate.

questions.stem: Which feature of a villus does NOT increase the rate of absorption?
options: A thick layer of muscle tissue beneath its surface
Microvilli on the surface of its epithelial cells
A dense network of blood capillaries in its core
An epithelium only one cell thick
questions.explanation: Microvilli increase the surface area, a one-cell-thick epithelium shortens the diffusion distance, and capillaries carry nutrients away to keep the gradient steep. A thick muscle layer would not help absorption.

questions.stem: Glucose is absorbed from the small intestine even when its concentration in the gut is lower than in the epithelial cells. Which process is involved, and what does it need?
options: Osmosis, needing water to move into the gut
Facilitated diffusion, needing a higher gut concentration
Active transport, needing energy from respiration
Diffusion, needing a large surface area only
questions.explanation: Moving glucose from low to high concentration requires active transport, which uses carrier proteins and energy from respiration. Diffusion, including facilitated diffusion, can only move substances down a concentration gradient.

questions.stem: Each villus contains a lacteal, a lymph capillary. Which nutrients mainly enter the lacteals?
options: Products of fat digestion
Glucose and other simple sugars
Amino acids
Mineral ions
questions.explanation: Fatty acids and glycerol are reassembled into fats in the epithelial cells and enter the lacteals as droplets, travelling in the lymph before reaching the blood. Sugars and amino acids enter the blood capillaries.

questions.stem: How are root hair cells suited to taking up water and mineral ions?
options: Long extensions give a large surface area in contact with soil water
A thick waxy cuticle stops water from leaking back out of the cell into the soil
Many chloroplasts supply glucose made by photosynthesis
Rigid lignin walls pump water inwards like the heart
questions.explanation: Root hairs are long, thin extensions of epidermal cells that greatly increase the surface area for absorption. They have no waxy cuticle and few or no chloroplasts, as they grow in the dark soil.

questions.stem: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis, but nitrate ions are taken up even when the soil has a lower nitrate concentration than the root. What does this tell you?
options: Nitrate uptake happens only through the stomata of leaves
Nitrate uptake is by active transport, which needs energy
Nitrate uptake is by osmosis, together with the water
Nitrate uptake is by diffusion from the cells into the soil
questions.explanation: Uptake against a concentration gradient requires energy from respiration and carrier proteins, so nitrate is absorbed by active transport. Osmosis refers only to water movement.

questions.stem: What is the functional unit of the human kidney that filters blood and forms urine?
options: The villus
The ureter
The nephron
The alveolus
questions.explanation: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, which filter the blood, reabsorb useful substances and produce urine. The ureter carries urine from the kidney to the bladder.

questions.stem: Which substances are normally filtered out of the blood into the Bowman's capsule?
options: Plasma proteins, glucose and urea
Water, glucose, salts and urea
Red blood cells and plasma proteins
White blood cells and platelets
questions.explanation: High pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules such as water, glucose, salts and urea into the capsule. Blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass through the filter.

questions.stem: Glucose is filtered into the nephron but is normally absent from urine. Why?
options: All of it is reabsorbed into the blood from the tubule
It is broken down and converted into urea inside the nephron tubule
It is too large to be filtered at the glomerulus
It is stored in the bladder until it is needed
questions.explanation: Glucose is small enough to be filtered, but in a healthy person all of it is reabsorbed, mainly in the proximal tubule, back into the blood. Glucose in urine can indicate uncontrolled diabetes.

questions.stem: Why is it important that the nephron both filters and reabsorbs, rather than simply removing urea from the blood?
options: Filtration happens only when the body has too much glucose in the blood
Filtration removes small molecules without selection, then useful ones are taken back
Filtration selects only urea, and reabsorption returns any urea to the blood
Reabsorption removes extra urea, while filtration returns water to the blood
questions.explanation: Filtration is non-selective: all small molecules pass into the nephron. Selective reabsorption then returns useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water, leaving wastes like urea in the urine.

questions.stem: How do some mangroves deal with the large amount of salt they take in from seawater?
options: They convert the salt into glucose in their chloroplasts
They release the salt as a gas through their stomata
Salt glands on their leaves excrete salt to the surface
Their roots pump salt into the phloem to feed the shoots
questions.explanation: Some mangroves, such as the grey mangrove, excrete salt through salt glands on their leaves, and some store salt in older leaves that are later shed. Plants can remove wastes or store them, since they have no excretory system like animals.

questions.stem: How do blood capillaries and lymph capillaries differ in their role in exchange?
options: Blood capillaries exchange materials with tissue fluid; lymph capillaries collect excess fluid
Blood capillaries collect excess fluid; lymph capillaries carry oxygen to all cells
Both carry red blood cells, but lymph capillaries flow away from the heart
Lymph capillaries pump blood, and blood capillaries carry only fats
questions.explanation: Fluid leaks from blood capillaries to form tissue fluid, through which materials are exchanged with cells. Lymph capillaries collect the excess tissue fluid and return it, as lymph, to the blood.

questions.stem: If lymph vessels in a person's leg are blocked, what would be expected?
options: Blood pressure in the leg arteries drops to zero
Tissue fluid builds up and the leg swells
The leg receives too much oxygen and turns red
Red blood cells leak out and form clots in the leg
questions.explanation: Normally, excess tissue fluid drains into lymph capillaries. If the lymph vessels are blocked, the fluid cannot drain away, so it accumulates and causes swelling. Red blood cells do not normally leave the capillaries.

questions.stem: Which blood vessels have walls only one cell thick, allowing exchange with body cells?
options: Venules
Capillaries
Arteries
Veins
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are a single layer of cells, giving a very short diffusion distance between blood and tissue fluid. Arteries and veins have thicker walls with muscle and elastic tissue.

questions.stem: What does xylem transport in a plant?
options: Water and mineral ions from the roots
Sugars from the leaves to the roots
Oxygen from the leaves to the roots
Starch from the tubers to the leaves
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions upwards from the roots to the stems and leaves. Phloem carries the products of photosynthesis, such as sucrose.

questions.stem: Which statement about the movement of water up the xylem is correct?
options: Water is pushed up only by gravity from the leaves
Each living xylem cell actively transports water on to the next cell above
Transpiration pulls a column of water held together by cohesion
Phloem pumps water upwards using energy from respiration
questions.explanation: Evaporation from leaves creates a pull (transpiration pull), and cohesion between water molecules, due to hydrogen bonding, keeps the column continuous up the xylem. Root pressure also pushes water up a little. Xylem cells are dead, so they cannot actively transport water.

questions.stem: What causes root pressure?
options: Phloem sap pushes water sideways into the xylem
Soil particles press on the roots and squeeze water into the root hairs
Ions moved into the xylem make water follow by osmosis
Evaporation from leaves pulls water up the stem
questions.explanation: Root cells actively move mineral ions into the xylem, lowering its water potential, so water enters by osmosis and builds up pressure that pushes water up. Transpiration pull is a separate, larger effect from the leaves.

questions.stem: A leafy shoot is set up in a potometer. Which change would most increase the rate of water uptake?
options: Placing a clear plastic bag over the shoot to trap moisture
Moving it to a cool, humid, still room in darkness
Moving it to a warm, dry, windy place in bright light
Covering its leaves with petroleum jelly on both surfaces
questions.explanation: Warmth, low humidity, wind and light (which opens stomata) all increase transpiration, which pulls more water up the shoot. Petroleum jelly blocks stomata, and a bag raises humidity, both reducing transpiration.

questions.stem: What is translocation in plants?
options: Loss of water vapour from the leaves through the stomata
Movement of gases through the air spaces in the leaf
Movement of sugars and other products of photosynthesis in the phloem
Movement of water and mineral ions upwards in the xylem
questions.explanation: Translocation is the transport of dissolved products of photosynthesis, mainly sucrose, and some mineral nutrients through the phloem. It can move materials up or down, from where they are made to where they are used or stored.

questions.stem: A potato plant moves sucrose from its leaves to its underground tubers, where it is stored as starch. Why is sucrose converted to starch in the tubers?
options: Starch is a waste product that the plant can no longer use
Starch is insoluble, so it stores energy without affecting osmosis
Starch is soluble, so it can be quickly carried back to the leaves
Starch is a mineral nutrient that the xylem cannot carry
questions.explanation: Starch is insoluble, so large amounts can be stored without drawing water into the cells by osmosis. Later it can be broken down to sugars for transport in the phloem, such as when the tuber sprouts.

questions.stem: Which lifestyle choice is most directly linked to damage of the alveoli and to lung cancer?
options: Regular aerobic exercise
Smoking tobacco
Drinking too much water
Eating a high-fibre diet
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke contains carcinogens and irritants that damage alveolar walls and the lining of airways, increasing the risk of emphysema and lung cancer. Regular exercise and a high-fibre diet support organ health.

questions.stem: A diet high in saturated fat can lead to fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries. Which effect on another system is most likely?
options: The kidneys filter more glucose from the blood, so the urine then contains fat
The villi absorb less fat, so the arteries clear again
Less oxygen reaches heart muscle, which can cause a heart attack
More oxygen reaches the lungs, raising the breathing rate
questions.explanation: Narrowed coronary arteries (atherosclerosis) reduce blood flow to the heart muscle, so it receives less oxygen and may be damaged in a heart attack. This shows how a lifestyle choice affects the circulatory system and, through it, the whole body.
